source_text: Illorum ergo primorum hominum, id est, tantum duorum, opitulari sibi laudem arbitratur ad distinctionem inter Manichaeos et Traducianos tenendam; qua opinione haud facile quidquam vel eminentius, vel impudentius offendi potest. Libertas, inquit, arbitrii, postquam se uti coepit, vires suas perdidit. Et ut conversi ad eum, pedetentim omnia perscrutemur; confiteris nempe primum hominem effectum esse arbitrio libero, bonumque a Deo conditum, nulla ab exordio peccati tabe pollutum; sed conditionis innocuae sponte deinceps praevaricatum, coactionem inevitabilem cunctis ex se oriundis intulisse peccandi. Hoc certe est dogma vestrum, quod nos de Manichaei coeno testamur expressum, qui et ipsius Adae naturam, licet de primae concretam flore substantiae, multo meliorem secutis, tamen malam naturaliter opinatur.
pass_a_gloss: The praise therefore of those first humans, that is of only two, he thinks helps him for holding a distinction between Manichaeans and Traducians; than which opinion hardly anything either more eminent or more shameless can be met. Freedom, he says, of decision, after it began to use itself, lost its powers. And that turned toward him we may search all things step by step; you confess indeed that the first human was made with a free decision, and founded good by God, polluted from the beginning by no wasting of sin; but thereafter having prevaricated by the will of an innocent condition, he brought an inevitable co-forcing of sinning upon all arising from himself. This certainly is your dogma, which we testify was expressed from Manichaeus's filth, who also opines the nature of Adam himself, although concreted from the flower of the first substance, much better than those following, nevertheless evil naturally.

lemmas.lexica: Julian's polemic label for teachers of tradux peccati
LS tradux=vine-shoot/layer; Blaise tradux peccati=transmission of sin by descent
Blaise Manichaeus; Julian's polemic label vs natural evil
LS naturalis; Blaise malum naturale=evil as a nature
LS arbitrium=judgment, free decision; Blaise liberum arbitrium
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself

pass_b_english: He thinks, therefore, that praising those first humans—just two people—helps him maintain a distinction between Manichaeans and advocates of inherited sin. It is hard to encounter anything more outrageous or shameless than this opinion. Freedom of choice, he says, lost its strength once it began to exercise itself.

Let us turn to him and carefully investigate each point. You admit, do you not, that the first human was made with free will, created good by God, and polluted by no corruption of sin at the outset? Yet, though his original condition was innocent, he afterward transgressed voluntarily and imposed on everyone to be born from him an unavoidable compulsion to sin. This is certainly your doctrine, which we testify was drawn from Mani’s mud. For Mani also regards Adam’s own nature as naturally evil, although formed from the flower of the first substance and far better than those who followed.

choices.why: Julian's polemic target is inherited sin as a natural evil (malum naturale), the vine-layer metaphor, not a later systematic 'original sin' slogan and not soul-traducianism as such.
rejected: original sin (later system as default gloss)
traducianism of the soul (not the load here)

choices.why: Glossary default: arbitrium is the decision-power, not a later Augustinian/Reformation free-will locus.
Julian's Manichaean charge: an evil that is a nature, not a will's act.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
